questions.title: Why did the court vacate the district court's judgment instead of simply affirming the dismissal?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural outcome here. The district court dismissed AFL's case for failure to state a claim, which sounds like a merits dismissal. But the D.C. Circuit vacated that judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Why does this distinction matter? If the result is that AFL loses either way, why does the appeals court bother vacating rather than just affirming? Is there some practical consequence I'm missing?

questions.title: When does a statute create an 'entitlement' to information sufficient for informational standing?
questions.question_body: The court says AFL can't establish informational standing because section 1216 creates no 'entitlement to receive information.' It cites cases like FEC v. Akins and Public Citizen v. DOJ where statutes did create such entitlements. How do I tell the difference? Section 1216(a)(3) uses the mandatory 'shall... conduct an investigation' - doesn't that suggest AFL has some right to have the investigation happen? What makes a statute create an entitlement versus just creating a procedural requirement?

questions.title: Why is the causal chain too attenuated when it involves independent actors not before the court?
questions.question_body: The court rejects AFL's first standing theory because the causal chain requires speculation about actions by MSPB and DOJ, who aren't parties to the case. The court cites FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine saying causation 'cannot rely on speculation about the unfettered choices made by independent actors not before the courts.' But doesn't almost any standing analysis involve some speculation about how third parties will react? Where exactly is the line between acceptable causation analysis and impermissible speculation about independent actors?

questions.title: How does Heckler v. Chaney apply when a statute uses mandatory language like 'shall'?
questions.question_body: The court cites Heckler v. Chaney for the principle that courts generally cannot compel agencies to exercise enforcement discretion. But section 1216(a)(3) says OSC 'shall... conduct an investigation' - that sounds mandatory, not discretionary. Does Heckler still apply even when Congress uses mandatory statutory language? Is there a difference between an agency's decision not to investigate at all versus its discretionary choices during an investigation?

questions.title: When do relaxed standing requirements apply to procedural injuries?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that when plaintiffs allege injury from violation of a procedural right designed to protect their threatened concrete interest, courts relax the imminence and redressability requirements. But the court says AFL doesn't satisfy 'even a relaxed standard' - and also says it need not decide whether these injuries are procedural or substantive. I thought the relaxed standard was specifically FOR procedural injuries. How can the court apply a relaxed standard without first deciding whether the injury is procedural? And what exactly does the plaintiff need to show under this relaxed standard?

questions.title: Why can't AFL's ongoing FOIA litigation against DOJ establish redressability?
questions.question_body: AFL's underlying FOIA lawsuit against DOJ is apparently still ongoing, with DOJ producing records. The court says any informational injury from DOJ's refusal to disclose is traceable to DOJ, not OSC. But if OSC investigated and found wrongdoing, couldn't that influence the FOIA litigation or pressure DOJ to produce more? The court mentions that redressability turns on 'how a judgment binds the parties, not whether its rationale might persuade actors not before the court.' But couldn't an OSC finding of arbitrary withholding be legally relevant in the FOIA case?

questions.title: What is the relationship between section 1216 investigations and section 1214 notice requirements?
questions.question_body: AFL argued that if OSC investigated under section 1216, it might provide the notices required under section 1214. The court notes that AFL 'acknowledges cases holding that OSC's decision whether to follow section 1214's procedural requirements in a section 1216 investigation is discretionary.' Does this mean section 1216 investigations are procedurally different from prohibited personnel practice investigations under section 1214? If OSC investigates a FOIA violation under 1216, what procedural rights (if any) does a complainant have?

questions.title: Why didn't the court reach the merits of whether section 552(a)(4)(F)(i) limits OSC's authority?
questions.question_body: The district court held that section 552(a)(4)(F)(i) doesn't limit OSC's power to investigate under section 1216, and that OSC's refusal to investigate was based on legal error. But the appeals court never addresses this - it just finds standing lacking. I thought courts were supposed to avoid constitutional questions when possible, but here the court reaches the constitutional standing issue instead of the statutory interpretation question. Isn't the statutory question about whether OSC misinterpreted its authority potentially dispositive?
